page8_img_1.png.title: Monthly accuracy metrics for the Recency reviewer-recommender model
page8_img_1.png.description: A time series (monthly) of four adjusted accuracy metrics for the Recency recommendation model: precision (red circles), recall (green squares), MRR (purple triangles) and the rate of empty recommendation lists (cyan diamonds). A vertical dashed line marks when the deployed model was switched to Recency+Size; the plot shows the Recency model’s metrics both before and after that deployment date. Pre- and post-change average values printed on the figure are: precision 0.474 → 0.457, recall 0.708 → 0.722, empty recommendation rate 0.172 → 0.152, and MRR 0.640 → 0.648. All metrics fluctuate month-to-month but the small differences across the model-change boundary lie within the observed monthly variance, indicating no clear discontinuity associated with the deployed model change.

page10_img_1.png.title: Monthly average reviewer recommendation counts (Recency vs Recency+Size)
page10_img_1.png.description: Scatter plot across monthly periods showing two measures of recommendation list size: grey circles are the average number of recommended reviewers per event (including events with no recommendations), and orange triangles are the average number of recommendations for events where the recommender produced at least one candidate. A vertical dashed line marks the deployment change from the Recency model (left) to the Recency+Size model (right). Numeric summaries printed on the plot show Recency produced on average 1.420 recommendations overall and 1.715 when non-zero, while Recency+Size produced 1.124 overall and 1.522 when non-zero, indicating a clear reduction in recommendation counts after the model change; month-to-month variation is small compared to this drop.

page19_img_1.png.title: Precision of reviewer recommendations vs. author tenure
page19_img_1.png.description: Scatter plot (Fig. 14) shows average precision on the y-axis against a maximum actor tenure threshold (years) on the x-axis; each point is the precision computed after discarding events whose change author has tenure above the threshold. Two series are plotted: grey circles for the Recency model and orange triangles for the Recency+Size model. Both models show higher precision for low-tenure authors (≈0.56 for Recency and ≈0.61 for Recency+Size near 0 years) that steadily declines as the tenure threshold increases and then stabilizes around 0.48–0.51 after about 5–6 years. The Recency+Size model maintains higher precision than Recency across all thresholds, and the authors note this pattern may reflect that less-experienced authors’ choices align better with recommendations (though causality is not established).

page11_img_1.png.title: Survey responses on reviewer recommendations at JetBrains and Microsoft
page11_img_1.png.description: Stacked Likert bars compare JetBrains and Microsoft respondents on four questions: whether they already know whom to pick as reviewer, whether recommendations are relevant, whether recommendations help pick a reviewer, and whether recommendations are irrelevant. The chart shows that most developers already know the reviewer in advance (JetBrains: 63% “Always” and 31% “Usually”; Microsoft: combined 92% “Always/Usually/Frequently”), and that JetBrains respondents report recommendations helping least (69% of JetBrains said recommendations “Never” help), whereas Microsoft responses are more mixed (about 30% “Never” or “Rarely” helpful and ~23% “Usually” or “Always” helpful). Both populations largely judge recommendations relevant more often than not, but only a small fraction (≈10% at Microsoft) find them relevant in all cases, reflecting that relevance does not translate into widespread perceived usefulness.

page5_img_1.png.title: Upsource code-review interface showing reviewers and inline comment
page5_img_1.png.description: Screenshot of the Upsource main review view for the file AggregationTest.java. The left panel shows metadata and participant controls: the author “Alice Doe”, an area for Reviewers with two avatars (John Lee, Will Roy) and a “+” to add more, Watchers, Timeline, and Files. The central pane displays the inline diff with a highlighted changed line containing Date joined = new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd z").parse("2016-05-01 UTC"); and an inline review comment from John Lee reading “Are you sure it is the right format?” with a 4m timestamp, Reply and Resolve actions. Top-right controls include a Side-by-side diff / Go to file button and small change counters (+1, −1); this interface exemplifies the integrated reviewer-selection and discussion context in which the paper’s deployed recommender presents one-click reviewer suggestions to authors.

page17_img_table_1.png.title: When developers find it hardest to choose code reviewers
page17_img_table_1.png.description: Table summarizing responses (273 answers, 344 tags) about the most difficult situations for selecting reviewers. The largest category is "Uncommon context" (163 tags, 47.4% of tags), reported by 146 respondents (53.5%), with sub-cases: not-usual area (92 responses, 33.7%), legacy code (40, 14.7%), and being a newcomer (31, 11.4%). The next major category is "Special ownership" (100 tags, 29.1%; 100 respondents, 36.6%), including unclear owner (47 responses, 17.2%), shared code (21, 7.7%), and development from scratch (20, 7.3%). Other notable categories are "Reviewer availability" (41 tags, 11.9%; 41 respondents, 15.0%) and smaller categories for "Uncommon impact" (22 tags, 6.4%) and "Uncommon content" (18 tags, 5.2%), indicating that lack of ownership/experience and unfamiliar code areas are the primary drivers of difficulty in choosing reviewers.

page13_img_1.png.title: Information developers consider when picking code reviewers
page13_img_1.png.description: Stacked horizontal bars show how often Microsoft developers consider 13 types of information when choosing a reviewer, with responses broken into four categories (I don’t consider it / I don’t consider but think it’s relevant / I sometimes consider it / I definitely consider it). The top factors are current involvement with the changed code (63% “definitely”, 28% “sometimes” → 91% at least sometimes), owning files in the changeset (70% definitely, 16% sometimes → 86%), and having previously made changes to the files (36% definitely, 46% sometimes → 82%). Mid-ranked factors include working in dependent areas, prior review history, opting in for reviews, and availability, while the least-used cues are physical proximity and current low activity (51–57% report they do not consider these and do not find them relevant). These proportions support the paper’s finding that developers mainly rely on involvement/ownership and recent contribution signals when selecting reviewers, whereas workload and office proximity are rarely used.

page7_img_1.png.title: Upsource reviewer recommendation workflow (example)
page7_img_1.png.description: A numbered workflow diagram showing how Upsource generates reviewer suggestions for a change (Review #CR-42) that modifies PoolUtil.java and Properties.kt. The tool retrieves the VCS change history for those files (step 2–3), the model scores candidate developers (example score table: Alice Doe 0.31, Jack Shaw 0.22, Will Roy 0.14, John Lee 0.12, James Foo 0.07), and then filters out the change author, current reviewers (Jack Shaw) and low-scoring users to produce up to three recommendations. The UI presents the remaining candidates (Alice Doe, Will Roy), the author (John Lee) clicks Alice from the popup, and an event is recorded with Alice Doe added as reviewer on 2017-08-16; a prior reviewer (Jack Shaw) was added on 2017-08-15. The figure illustrates the end-to-end, event-level process (history → scoring → filtering → UI → reviewer-add event) that the paper evaluates when measuring per-addition precision and recall.

page10_img_2.png.title: Coverage of recommended vs. picked reviewers for two recommendation models
page10_img_2.png.description: Bar chart comparing five user-coverage metrics for the Recency (left) and Recency+Size (right) recommendation periods: “active”, “recommended”, “picked”, “intersection”, and “match”. For the Recency model (133 active developers) the bars show 116 recommended (87%), 115 picked (86%), 90 in the intersection (68%), and 80 match (60%). For Recency+Size (179 active) the values are 120 recommended (67%), 135 picked (75%), 100 intersection (56%), and 94 match (53%). Although Recency+Size recommends a smaller fraction of the active pool (67% vs. 87%), it produces larger absolute intersection and match counts and higher follow-through among its recommended set (intersection/recommended ≈ 83% vs. 78%, match/recommended ≈ 78% vs. 69%), suggesting its smaller recommendation subset is more likely to be selected by users.

page6_img_1.png.title: Overview of the mixed-method research workflow for RQ1–RQ3
page6_img_1.png.description: A schematic flowchart divided into two dashed areas labeled for JetBrains (top) and Microsoft (bottom) shows how data sources and analyses produce results for the three research questions. On the JetBrains side, icons for “Reviews history” and “Reproduced recommendations” feed a “Quantitative analysis” (gears) box that produces the RQ1 results; alongside this, interview and a small JetBrains survey feed into RQ2 results. The Microsoft section shows a larger “Survey 2” box (Likert + open questions) whose responses go through iterative tagging and analysis to produce RQ3 results. Arrows between the blocks indicate that a central “Analysis and discussion” step integrates findings across the quantitative reproduction (over ~21,000 JetBrains reviews) and the qualitative surveys (including the larger Microsoft survey of ~507 responses) to draw the study’s conclusions.

page15_img_2.png.title: Information developers report missing when selecting reviewers
page15_img_2.png.description: This table (from 74 valid open-ended Microsoft survey responses) categorizes the kinds of information developers would like but cannot obtain when choosing reviewers, reporting both tag counts (90 total tags) and the number/percentage of responses mentioning each category. The top three missing categories are Past contributions (25 responses, 33.8%), Reviewer qualities (24 responses, 32.4%), and Ownership (21 responses, 28.4%); the most-cited single subitem is “Past authors of changes to code” (18 responses, 24.3%). Smaller but non-negligible needs include Knowledge (9 responses, 12.2%) and Dependency information (5 responses, 6.8%), indicating demand for history/ownership and reviewer reputation/availability data that tools currently do not surface easily.

page22_img_1.png.title: Author portrait photograph in paper's author-bios section
page22_img_1.png.description: A square color head-and-shoulders photograph showing a young adult male with light blond hair, light facial stubble, and a neutral expression, facing the camera and wearing a dark hoodie. The image is tightly cropped around the face and shoulders and occupies the left column of an author-biography layout; to its right is a multi-line text block with a bold heading and several lines of biographical information about an author’s academic background and research interests. The portrait is presented as the photographic accompaniment to an author bio in the paper (i.e., part of the authors’ profile section).

page9_img_1.png.title: Monthly accuracy and empty-recommendation rates before and after model change
page9_img_1.png.description: Time-series scatter plot of four monthly metrics for non-empty recommendation events from Jan 2015 to early 2017: precision (red circles), recall (green squares), empty recommendation rate (cyan diamonds), and MRR (purple triangles). A vertical dashed line marks the deployment switch from the Recency model (left period) to the Recency+Size model (right period); period averages are annotated: Recency — precision 0.474, recall 0.708, empty rate 0.172, MRR 0.640; Recency+Size — precision 0.492, recall 0.662, empty rate 0.262, MRR 0.612. The plot shows Recency+Size is more conservative (higher empty recommendation rate) with slightly higher precision but lower recall and MRR, and no abrupt change in monthly values at the model switch (differences lie within monthly variance).

page15_img_1.png.title: Survey: Difficulty obtaining information for reviewer selection
page15_img_1.png.description: Stacked-bar responses from Microsoft developers show how easy or hard different kinds of information are to obtain when choosing a reviewer. The hardest-to-get items are review-history related: “Has previously reviewed files in the changeset” (31% report Difficult, 13% Very difficult, 4% Impossible) and “Has previously requested reviews on files in the changeset” (26% Difficult, 14% Very difficult, 7% Impossible) — together about 43–48% of respondents rate these as somewhat or very difficult. Information about code-dependency (e.g., “Works in an area dependent on files in the changeset”) is also relatively hard (25% Difficult, 16% Very difficult, 5% Impossible ≈ 46%). By contrast, authorship/change history and ownership are generally easy to obtain: “Has previously made changes to files in the changeset” is rated I already know/Very easy/Easy by 8%/40%/28% (≈76% easy), “Owns files in the changeset” by 21%/20%/19% (≈60% easy), and physical proximity is overwhelmingly known (50% “I already know it”, 24% Very easy). These results align with the paper’s finding that review-history and dependency information are often missing or harder to retrieve, while authorship and ownership are commonly accessible.

page14_img_table_1.png.title: Information types developers consider when selecting reviewers
page14_img_table_1.png.description: This table summarizes tags from 270 open-ended Microsoft survey responses (373 total tags) about additional information developers consider when choosing reviewers. The largest category is "Knowledge" (85 tags; 80 responses, 29.6%), with "Knowledge of area" most cited (42 tags; 42 responses, 15.6%). A substantial fraction report "None" (69 tags; 68 responses, 25.2%) — commonly sending the request to the whole team (50 responses) — while "Seniority" (66 tags; 62 responses, 23.0%) and "Stakeholder" (63 tags; 60 responses, 22.2%) are also frequent. Other notable categories are "Reviewer qualities" (54 tags; 50 responses, 18.5%), driven by "Reviewer is thorough" (34 responses, 12.6%), and "Ownership" (36 tags; 34 responses, 12.6%), led by "Area ownership" (18 responses, 6.7%).

page8_img_2.png.title: Monthly precision, recall, MRR and empty-rate for Recency+Size recommender (2015–2017)
page8_img_2.png.description: Time series of four evaluation metrics for reviewer recommendations plotted by month: precision (red circles), recall (green squares), empty recommendation rate (cyan diamonds), and MRR (purple triangles). A vertical dashed line marks the point when the deployed model changed; horizontal dashed lines show period averages. The figure annotates average values before the change (precision 0.464, recall 0.612, empty rate 0.267, MRR 0.557) and after the change (precision 0.492, recall 0.662, empty rate 0.262, MRR 0.612). Overall the monthly trajectories fluctuate but show no abrupt shift at the model-change boundary, i.e., differences between periods lie within normal month-to-month variance.
